UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION




DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC            Docket No. P-15424-000




CONSOLIDATED ANSWER OF APPLICANT

DEEPGREEN WESTERN PASSAGE SPV LLC

TO MOTIONS TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS




Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,

18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213, DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC (“Applicant”)

respectfully submits this Consolidated Answer to the timely Motions to Intervene and

Comments submitted by the Center for Biological Diversity (“CBD”), the

Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik (“Tribe”), the City of Eastport, Maine (“City”), the

Eastport Port Authority (“Port Authority”), the Conservation Law Foundation (“CLF”), the

New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association (“NEFSA”), Save Passamaquoddy

Bay, and other commenters.

To the extent this Answer addresses protests or public comments, Applicant respectfully

moves for leave to answer, as this single submittal clarifies statutory authority,

eliminates repetitive briefing, corrects factual misapprehensions, and ensures an

accurate administrative record to assist the Commission in evaluating the application.
                                                                                         1
 Applicant does not oppose party intervention by CBD, the Tribe, the City, the Port

Authority, CLF, NEFSA, or Save Passamaquoddy Bay. Applicant files this response to

establish the governing statutory framework under Section 4(f) of the Federal Power Act

(FPA), 16 U.S.C. § 797(f), and to address specific legal and regulatory assertions raised

in the record.

I. PROCEDURAL STATUS

On February 11, 2026, Applicant filed an application for a preliminary permit pursuant to

Section 4(f) of the FPA, 16 U.S.C. § 797(f), to examine the feasibility of the DeepGreen

Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project. On June 8, 2026, and

July 30, 2026, Applicant submitted amendments and supplemental filings defining an

initial Phase 1 study area of approximately 27.1 acres off Kendall Head with an initial

pilot capacity of 1 to 5 MW.

On August 25, 2026, the Commission published notice of the accepted application in the

Federal Register, establishing an intervention and comment deadline. Timely

interventions and comments were submitted by the aforementioned parties.




II. THE STATUTORY FUNCTION OF A PRELIMINARY PERMIT

The primary objections raised by commenters rest upon a fundamental misconception:

that the requested preliminary permit authorizes construction, physical disturbance of

the seabed, operational thermal discharge, or vessel exclusion zones. Under

established Commission practice, it does not.



                                                                                           2
 A. A Preliminary Permit Grants Priority Only and Authorizes No Construction

Section 4(f) of the FPA serves a single administrative purpose: to maintain application

priority while the permittee investigates project feasibility. 16 U.S.C. § 797(f). A

preliminary permit does not authorize an applicant to disturb the seabed, install subsea

cradles or compute pods, dredge cables, discharge cooling water, establish navigational

exclusion zones, or occupy municipal or private property.

Because a preliminary permit authorizes no physical works, its issuance does not

constitute a major federal action under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA),

42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C), nor does it trigger formal consultation under Section 7 of the

Endangered Species Act (ESA), 16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2), or incidental take

authorizations under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), 16 U.S.C. § 1371. If

Applicant ultimately conducts field survey activities that require independent federal or

state authorizations (such as authorizations from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers or

NOAA Fisheries), Applicant will secure all required permits and comply with all

applicable environmental protocols prior to commencing in-water work.

B. Licensing-Stage Detail Is Not Required at the Preliminary Permit Stage

Under 18 C.F.R. § 4.81(c), an application for a preliminary permit requires only a

general description and proposed schedule of studies. The detailed micro-siting

analyses, operational acoustic modeling, and definitive mitigation protocols demanded

by commenters are precisely what the FPA reserves for development during the permit

term under Commission-supervised pre-filing consultation.




                                                                                            3
 III. RESPONSE TO SPECIFIC STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS

A. Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik

Applicant recognizes the Tribe’s historic, cultural, and sustenance connection to the

waters of the Western Passage and does not contest its intervention.

The Tribe asserts that Maine submerged lands leasing rules under 12 M.R.S. § 1862

and 01-670 C.M.R. ch. 53, § 1.6.A limit non-commercial fishing structures to 2,000

square feet, arguing this statutorily precludes the project under Hudson River-Black

River Regulating District, 33 FERC ¶ 61,122 (1985). That decision, however, involved

an express constitutional bar in the New York State Constitution governing state forest

preserves. Under Part I of the FPA, the Commission maintains comprehensive authority

over the study and licensing of hydrokinetic facilities in navigable waters. State

administrative leasing guidelines do not operate as an automatic threshold bar to

Commission jurisdiction or to feasibility investigations under a preliminary permit.

Furthermore, under 18 C.F.R. § 4.81, a preliminary permit applicant is not required to

hold property rights, littoral rights, or state submerged land leases prior to permit

issuance. Evaluating landfall routes, transmission corridors, and real property

requirements is a core objective of the preliminary permit term.

B. City of Eastport and Eastport Port Authority

Applicant welcomes the participation of the City of Eastport and the Eastport Port

Authority.




                                                                                          4
 The City notes that on September 9, 2026, the City Council enacted local ordinance

provisions intended to prohibit data center facilities. Under Part I of the FPA, local

zoning ordinances cannot preempt Commission jurisdiction or bar federal preliminary

permit studies in navigable waters.

In Exhibit A of its filing, the City identified four alternative requests if the permit is

granted: (1) early consultation; (2) advance notice of field studies; (3) environmental

evaluations; and (4) respect for municipal property. Applicant agrees with these

principles: Applicant will provide advance informational notice to City officials regarding

offshore survey schedules, coordinate with emergency personnel and harbor pilots, and

confirms that a preliminary permit confers no authority to enter City-owned property

without municipal consent.

C. Conservation Law Foundation (CLF)

Applicant does not oppose CLF’s Motion to Intervene.

CLF contends that the Commission should deny the permit because prospective state

data center moratoria and local opposition will make it difficult for Applicant to satisfy the

requirements of Section 9 of the FPA, 16 U.S.C. § 802(a)(2). Section 9 requirements

govern formal license applications, not preliminary permits. Commission regulations

under 18 C.F.R. § 4.81 do not require an applicant to demonstrate final compliance with

state land laws or local zoning at the preliminary permit threshold. Speculation

regarding vetoed state legislation (L.D. 307) or proposed future moratoria provides no

legal basis to deny a preliminary permit.




                                                                                              5
 Moreover, CLF’s references to large-scale thermal dilution zones and widespread

seabed disturbance are inapplicable. Applicant formally amended its study boundary to

an initial 27.1-acre footprint for a 1 to 5 MW pilot array. A preliminary permit authorizes

zero thermal discharge and zero construction.

D. New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association (NEFSA) and Maine Department

of Marine Resources (MEDMR)

NEFSA raises concerns regarding potential gear conflicts with lobster traps, scallop

dragging, acoustic displacement of groundfish, and loss of fishing access. A preliminary

permit establishes no safety exclusion zones and restricts no commercial fishing activity.

In its filing, NEFSA requests that Applicant consult with NEFSA, NOAA Fisheries, and

the Maine Department of Marine Resources (MEDMR) in developing study plans, and

provide periodic progress reports. On October 23, 2026, MEDMR filed a Notice of

Intervention pursuant to its statutory authority under 12 M.R.S. § 6021.

Applicant does not oppose MEDMR’s Notice of Intervention and welcomes the Agency's

formal participation. Applicant agrees with this consultative approach. During the

preliminary permit term, Applicant will coordinate closely with MEDMR, NOAA Fisheries,

and local fishing organizations to align survey schedules, avoid gear entanglement, and

utilize state and local marine science in formulating study protocols.




                                                                                              6
 E. Center for Biological Diversity (CBD)

CBD argues that the application lacks specific survey parameters and requests that the

Commission require additional scientific desktop studies under 18 C.F.R. § 4.32(g)(7)

and initiate ESA Section 7 and MMPA processes prior to permit issuance.

CBD’s procedural demands invert the statutory process. Commission regulations under

18 C.F.R. § 4.32(g)(7) govern study requests during the licensing and pre-filing stages,

not the preliminary permit application stage. Issuance of a preliminary permit authorizes

no physical survey work that could take or harass marine mammals.

During the permit term, non-invasive bathymetric and current mapping will be planned in

consultation with resource agencies, incorporating standard protected species

protocols—including qualified protected species observers (PSOs), passive acoustic

monitoring (PAM), and vessel speed limits—in accordance with federal guidelines.

F. Save Passamaquoddy Bay and Oceana

Save Passamaquoddy Bay filed a Motion to Intervene and comments, and Oceana

submitted comments expressing concern regarding localized thermal effects and

benthic disruption. Applicant does not oppose Save Passamaquoddy Bay's intervention.

As detailed above, a preliminary permit authorizes no physical works, construction, or

thermal discharge. Rigorous hydrodynamic and thermal modeling will occur during the

study term under Commission pre-filing procedures, ensuring full environmental data is

compiled prior to any license application.




                                                                                           7
 IV. CONCLUSION

The comments and objections presented provide no lawful basis under the Federal

Power Act to deny or delay the preliminary permit application. Applicant respectfully

requests that the Commission:

1. Grant the timely motions to intervene filed in this proceeding;

2. Reject the requests to dismiss or deny the application; and

3. Issue the preliminary permit for Project No. P-15424-000.

VERIFICATION AND SIGNATURE

Pursuant to 18 C.F.R. § 385.2005, the undersigned certifies that he is an authorized

representative of DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC; that he has read this filing

and knows its contents; that the facts stated herein are true to the best of his

knowledge, information, and belief; and that this submittal is warranted by existing law

and filed in good faith.

Respectfully submitted,

/Louis Wolfson/
